t:
The provisions of sections 102(b)(3) and 304(c) are enacted—

    (1) 
as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the House of Representatives and the Senate, respectively, and as such they shall be considered as part of the rules of such House, respectively, and such rules shall supersede other rules only to the extent that they are inconsistent therewith; and
 
    (2) 
with full recognition of the constitutional right of either House to change such rules (so far as relating to such House) at any time, in the same manner, and to the same extent as in the case of any other rule of each House.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the word "rulemaking" signals agency rulemaking with public comment. Here it refers to the constitutional power of each House of Congress to set its own internal procedural rules, and Congress is inside the federal government. No state, tribe, expert, company, or member of the public is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue, so there is no participation.
fable.s: as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the House of Representatives and the Senate, respectively, and as such they shall be considered as part of the rules of such House

qwen_block.w: This section describes the enactment of internal rules for the House of Representatives and the Senate. Congress is part of the federal government, and internal legislative procedures or rulemaking by Congress do not constitute participation by outside parties. There is no mention of consultation with states, the public, or other non-federal entities.
qwen_block.s: The provisions of sections 102(b)(3) and 304(c) are enacted— (1) as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the House of Representatives and the Senate, respectively, and as such they shall be considered as part of the rules of such House, respectively

opus.w: Here "rulemaking power" means each chamber of Congress setting its own internal rules. It does not mean a federal agency issuing regulations, which would bring in the public. Every actor in the section (the House and the Senate) is inside the federal government. No state, expert, company or member of the public is consulted or given a role, so this is not participation.
opus.s: as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the House of Representatives and the Senate, respectively, and as such they shall be considered as part of the rules of such House
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** The section says "rulemaking power," and the definition counts required rulemaking as participation. That reading fails here. This is the standard clause about Congress's own internal procedural rules. It is not agency rulemaking with notice and comment. Only the House and Senate are involved, and both are inside the federal government. No outside party is brought into any decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section describes the enactment of rules for the House of Representatives and the Senate. Since Congress is defined as being inside the federal government, and the text only concerns internal legislative rules and powers, there is no involvement of parties outside the federal government. The definition explicitly excludes interactions solely within the federal government (including Congress) from being classified as participation.
qwen_chat.s: as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the House of Representatives and the Senate, respectively, and as such they shall be considered as part of the rules of such House, respectively
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the text mentions the "House of Representatives" and the "Senate," it involves external bodies. However, the definition explicitly states that Congress, its committees, and its members are INSIDE the federal government. Therefore, any procedural rules or interactions strictly between these internal bodies do not constitute participation with outside parties.
